_about: Every number the checker uses is kept in this one file, and nowhere else. Each number comes with the reason for it. If someone asks "why 98.5%?", point here. The values follow common practice for fish DNA tests. They were NOT adjusted to make any sample pass.

min_length.why: The fish DNA piece we read is about 160 to 190 letters long. A piece under 100 letters is too short to tell close fish apart, so it is set aside.

max_n_percent.why: N means the machine could not read a letter. More than 2% of N in a short piece means 3 or more unreadable letters in the very part that tells fish apart.

min_mean_quality.why: Q20 means about 1 mistake in every 100 letters. This is the usual lowest level for this kind of test. It only applies to FASTQ files, because FASTA files carry no quality marks. The result says so.

min_complexity_entropy.why: This measures how varied the letters are. Below 1.5, one or two letters (like AAAAAA) fill the piece. That is not real fish DNA.

min_read_count.why: A DNA code seen only once is almost always a copying mistake of a real code. Setting such codes aside is standard practice.

identity_floor.why: If a piece is less than 80% alike to every fish on the list, it is not recognisable as fish DNA at all. It is set aside as unrelated and not sent for checking.

identity_species.why: To name a fish for sure, a piece must be at least 98.5% alike to the best fish on the list. Studies of this gene region commonly use 98 to 99%, so 98.5% sits in the middle.

min_species_margin.why: If the best fish and the next-best different fish are within 1 point of each other, we cannot honestly pick one. The piece goes to a person to check.

human_identity.why: The test can also copy human DNA. A piece that is 95% or more like human DNA is treated as human contamination and set aside.

unknown_max_confidence.why: An unknown can never look confirmed. Its match score is capped here, however good the closest match looks.

confidence_max_known.why: No answer is ever shown as 100% sure. The list of known fish is not complete, and a perfect match to the wrong fish is still possible.

min_detection_reads.why: A fish backed by fewer than 10 DNA pieces is shown as a trace, not as found. A few stray pieces often cross over between samples in the machine.

retake_min_kept_fraction.why: If under 10% of the DNA is usable, the test has mostly failed, so collect a new sample. An earlier version used 50%. Real deep-tested river samples showed that 70% off-target DNA is only a reason for care, not for throwing the sample away. The number of usable pieces below is the main test.

caution_max_dropped_fraction.why: If 25% to 50% of the DNA is lost, the sample is not useless, but it was a poor test (for example, lots of leftover test chemicals). The verdict is "Use with care" and the loss is shown, not hidden.

retake_min_kept_reads.why: With under 1,000 usable pieces we cannot describe which fish live there. A fish that makes up 0.5% would have only 5 pieces. This is the main "collect a new sample" test.

share_tolerance_factor.why: Some fish DNA copies better than others, so a measured share is never exact. A share within 3 times of the published share counts as consistent. Outside that range it is flagged.

season_months.why: This rule turns a collection month into a season. In the Pearl River area, the hot wet summer is April to September and the cool dry winter is October to March. Change it here for another region.

alert_latency_seconds.why: The challenge asks for an alert within seconds of a sample being processed. Each alert records how long it took, and this is the limit it is judged against.

max_unique_ratio_for_singleton_rule.unit: fraction of reads that are distinct
max_unique_ratio_for_singleton_rule.why: The "seen once means a mistake" rule only works when true copies are identical, which happens when every piece starts and ends at the same place. If more than half of the pieces are all different, a code seen once says nothing about mistakes. Then the rule is skipped and fish are counted piece by piece.

species_identity_by_marker.why: The cutoff to name a fish depends on the gene region. 12S has short DNA with few differences between fish, so it uses 98.5%. COI and 16S use 97%, the usual cutoff for these genes, and the one the authors of the fish-egg data used themselves.
